doc.title: David Torkanowsky interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019

chapter: Feel, skank and the New Orleans way
title: Swing versus straight eighth notes
summary: Torkanowsky explains the movable eighth note, how he teaches drummers the swing cymbal pattern, and who straightened out the feel (Horace Silver, Professor Longhair, Dr. John).

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: And I want to start with an odd question. It’s not a question it’s like can we talk about eighth notes?
When I was listening to you play, you did “Body and Soul” but you did a tune before that and I didn’t catch the name of it, it might have just been a —
It could have been an extemporaneous — I can’t think of what to play let me play something until I think of something.

Exactly. But you went through, the feel of the music changed as you progressed. And I think it has a lot to do with the series of eighth notes, whether they’re straight, whether they’re really swingy.

Well listen you know jazz was the popular music of a certain time. And then at some point rock & roll became the popular music. Now what was the transition? Well the eighth note was carrying the water. So in jazz music the eighth note we consider to be the first and last of a triplet [scats]. You know it’s interesting, when I teach young drummers how to swing on a cymbal I teach them, “Draw a quarter note on the left hand — draw a quarter note here, a dotted eighth here, and a sixteenth here. And put your stick right on that. Sorry. Put the quarter note here, dotted eighth here, sixteenth here. [Scats] and keep that rhythm. Keep that pattern. Now as you go faster, that becomes more eighth notes and the pattern becomes small [scats]. As you go slower the pattern becomes wider and this sixteenth note moves closer to the quarter note. [Scats]. Now that’s the way old cats used to play a ballad. Young cats rarely cross the triplet [scats]. Dig? But you know the pattern is still the same. And so what happens? Two things happen. First of all, a little more arm.

It’s swinging. Secondly, you have to [scats] on the backbeat you have to lift the stick and travel so that puts it — that makes the cymbal pattern swing. So that illustrates the movable eighth note. Now I think what you’re asking me is, in swing [scats] you know the funky players, Phil Woods for example, he would straighten out eighth notes because that made him sound funky. Horace Silver, the two fathers of funk to me are Horace Silver and Professor Longhair. Professor Longhair comes more out of a Caribbean rumba tradition. But and Horace Silver [scats] he was one of the first cats to straighten out the eighth notes. Now what you heard me play on that WWOZ post is kind of straight eighth notes with a little junk to it. Now if you ever heard of J.C. Heard play a bossa nova it was [scats] and it would kind of stretch the swing eighth notes, but somewhere between swing and straight, and you know where that is and you know it’s up to personal discretion, but it’s stretched eighth notes. Dr. John did the same thing [scats], and that’s kind of the way Smoky Johnson in New Orleans started playing funk. These cats all came out of a jazz tradition. Kind of shuffle became straight eighth notes. So it’s in that area that I like to explore because it puts a tear into the music. Now I’ve done straight recording sessions where they want me to play very precise. And I think I’m playing straight eighth notes and the producer says, “Hey man, it’s cool, but can you not swing it so much?” I didn’t realize I was. So I hope that answers your question.
